However, a 2020 study conducted by Dr Schoenfeld found that whether we train with low, moderate, or high-rep sets, it doesn’t have much of an impact on how much muscle we build or in which muscle fibre type gets that growth. So, as the research currently stands, it seems like we can bulk up our bigger fast-twitch muscle fibres just as well with moderate and high-rep training. There’s a fairly good explanation for this, too. Mechanical tension is the main driver of muscle growth in both our fast-twitch and slow-twitch muscle fibres, and so we can build muscle either by increasing the magnitude or duration of the tension. If we lift heavier weights for fewer reps, the magnitude is higher but the duration is lower, and vice versa. This explanation also hints at why very-low-rep sets don’t produce much muscle growth per set—because the slightly higher magnitude of the mechanical tension is dwarfed by the much higher duration of higher-rep sets. passages.text: Building muscle does not require complicated workouts or restrictive eating plans. Effective hypertrophy programming requires an understanding of the physiological adaptations that drive muscle growth and the training variables that influence those adaptations. This guide examines the science of muscle growth and provides personal trainers with evidence-based strategies for designing hypertrophy-focused programs. Topics include training volume, exercise selection, progressive overload, recovery, and programming considerations that support long-term muscular development. Heather Cherry NBC-HWC, IC-FHS, CPT, NTP What Drives Muscle Growth? Muscle growth, also known as hypertrophy, occurs when the body adapts to the demands placed on it during resistance training. When a client performs resistance exercises, the muscles experience mechanical tension that creates a signal for the body to repair and strengthen muscle tissue. In response to that challenge, the body increases muscle protein synthesis (MPS), the physiological process of repairing and building muscle proteins. During this process, amino acids from dietary protein are used to repair existing muscle tissues and build new muscle proteins. Hypertrophy occurs when the body builds more muscle tissue than it breaks down.
